subject: Residual covariances in IRT vs. SEM/FA

messages.author: c2e4e73074071c1f
messages.subject: Residual covariances in IRT vs. SEM/FA
parts:
I'm converting some IRT models into SEM models and vice versa with software such as lavaan. I wanted to make sure I understood how my lavaan model relates to the IRT models. Sorry if this is too much "trying to understand the model I'm coding in lavaan" than "how to lavaan."

Suppose I collect the responses to the same 3 items from the same N subjects at 2 measurement occasions (T = t1, t2). I fit a "longitudinal CFA" with 2 correlated factors (F1, F2), where F1 loads on the three t1 items and F2 loads on the three t2 items. Crucially, I estimate covariances between t1 and t2 residual variances for the 3 items.

De Boeck and Wilson (2004)'s discussion (Ch.10) of residual dependence in IRT models  suggest that e.g. a 2-PL IRT model could include  (a) subject-occasion random intercepts and (b) subject random intercepts to capture the 2 correlated factors. Is modeling correlated residuals across multiple occasions of the same item by assuming multivariate normality of the errors (as in the CFA) roughly equivalent to estimating (1) item-occasion random intercepts and (2) item random intercepts in an IRT model? As the intercepts are at different levels, I can't just sample them from a bivariate normal -- although I could do that if I just wanted (1).

messages.author: ac9e1459001ea58d
messages.subject: Re: Residual covariances in IRT vs. SEM/FA
parts:
The multilevel and structural equation modeling formulations of IRT are both to some extent "tricks" to do IRT in a system that was not designed for it. They both work fine (for 1PL and 2PL anyway), but a lot of things are easier to understand if you try to figure out what lavaan and/or glmer do in terms of the traditional IRT model.

In lavaan, IRT item difficulty is obtained from the factor loadings (lambda) and tresholds (tau). Unless you are fixing the loadings for the first factor to be identical to the loadings of the second, I would therefore imagine you automatically get an item difficulty that can differ for each occasion.

Mind you, it's entirely possible that I've misunderstood your question, in which case my apologies, I'm not an IRT expert by any means.

Best,

Stijn

messages.author: 9b7a59c6f2d552cc
messages.subject: Re: Residual covariances in IRT vs. SEM/FA
parts:
Bengt Muthén worked on integrating IRT and SEM/FA models and provides some good statistical and theoretical understanding of how thresholds work.
As i understand an IRT threshold is the ability/difficulty point at which the probability of answering one ordinal option switches to teh next ordinal option in Likert-type rating scales.
have a look at
Muthén, B. (1984). A general structural equation model with dichotomous, ordered categorical, and continuous latent variable indicators. Psychometrika, 49(1), 115-132. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02294210
Muthén, B. O., Kao, C.-F., & Burstein, L. (1991). Instructionally sensitive psychometrics: Application of a new IRT-based detection technique to mathematics achievement test items. Journal of Educational Measurement, 28(1), 1-22. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1745-3984.1991.tb00340.x

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: Re: Residual covariances in IRT vs. SEM/FA
parts:
They can be equivalent models. Such as these 2 are

mod1 <- '
f1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
f2 =~ x5 + x6 + x7 + x8
x1 ~~ x5
'

mod1 <- '
f1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
f2 =~ x5 + x6 + x7 + x8
 fres =~ a*x1 + a*x5
'
